messages.author: 061e4134cde5bdc7
messages.subject: missing year in dynamic model
parts:
Hy everyone,

I have 3 years of data, 2009, 2010 and 2013. 
1) Can I use the multiseason model for this unequal interval information?
2) How the model interprets the lack of information on the years 2011 and 2012? Can I use any correction factor?

Regards,

Marina

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] missing year in dynamic model
parts:
hi Marina,
 In this case you should use a  model that has a sepearate set of parameters for the 2010-2013 interval because you should expect more colonization or extinction over a 3 year period.
regards
andy

parts:
Dear Marina,

the dynamic occupancy model can be described as a four-fold logistic regression, or a generalised linear model with binomial distribution. Both your questions are really more general than the dynamic occupancy model and have simply to do with how we fit and interpret covariates in GLMs.

Hence, a good start would be any accessible introduction to GLMs, perhaps one of Crawley's books or a Zuur ?

Kind regards  --  Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] missing year in dynamic model
parts:
hi unmarkers and hello again, Marina,

I believe that a large part of the problems that people have with a package such as unmarked stems from the fact that a linear model must be specified: what do parameters mean, how do I combine the effects of two or more covariates, how can I get predictions (e.g., in a plot of survival probability against some covariate).

These problems have nothing to do with the specific kind of model, but are much more fundamental. They have to do with the linear model, which is the usual way in which we specify effects of discrete or continuous explanatory variables in our analyses. I am convinced that with a better grasp of the "applied fundamentals" of linear models and generalised linear models (only major thing there to understand is the link function) we can get a MUCH better understanding of hierarchical models such as those fit in unmarked. Indeed, half of the power of modern statistical modeling with packages such as MARK, PRESENCE, unmarked or even with the BUGS programming language consists of you being able to specify linear models in a clever way.

I haven't researched about accessible intros of the linear model and GLMs for ecologists. (Probably somebody should write an intro book for ecologists.) However, one of the best that I have ever seen is Evan Cooch's intro to linear models in his Gentle Introduction to Mark (http://www.phidot.org/software/mark/docs/book/, and then choose chapter 6). Of course, for people interested in the models in unmarked, you may have to do some mental translation, for instance, from survival probabilities in a CJS model to occupancy probability in an occupancy model, but the right-hand side of the equation, the linear model, stays the same, regardless of what's on the left-hand side.

Kind regards  --  Marc
